title: Part 2
text: slope. Together, they widened the gap, opening the small tunnel up to the outside air stone by stone, until David’s face came into view. Pale. Dust-caked. Blood seeping from his temple. But there was a pulse. It fluttered weakly beneath Dwight’s fingers — thready, irregular, but definitely there. Felix threw another stone off to the side, trying to sort out just how bad of an angle David was pinned at. Now that he had a better view, he could spot the edge of a much longer piece than the stones they had been digging at crossing over his collarbone. It seemed to be bracing the worst of the upper pile from digging too sharply into his torso, but there was no way to tell from here how far down it reached. For all he knew, David’s legs could be absolute pulp further down, without this slab protecting them. Some of these stones were insanely heavy and sharp. It was a good thing this larger piece had been preventing those sharp edges from cutting into vital organs. The slab would have taken all that weight and spread it out, instead of letting it stab straight down. Less of a battering and more... Nudging Dwight to the side, Felix crouched to work a hand down along his collarbone, trying to get under the slab. The muscles under his hand were lightly flexing in shallow, sporadic bursts against the weight above. The pressure had been spread out over his entire chest, compressing him down against the sand with every piece that fell from above. The geometry clicked. That slab was at the bottom of the pile. It wasn’t new to the collapse — it has been there from the start. Felix stared at David’s half-buried body, heart thudding, brain kicking into gear. The compression hadn’t just happened at the end — it had been building. For minutes , maybe longer. That stupid, stupid man hadn’t said a word. He’d held it all in. Let it get worse. Let it crush him while they were trying to help. Of course the panic had hit. Of course he had snapped. Anyone would have after that long. “You absolute idiot,” Felix hissed, shoving himself to his feet. He had to get that weight up and off David’s chest. He needed something sturdy. Anything. He spun in place for a moment, doing a rapid inventory of the area around him and coming up empty. His eyes paused on a nearby doorway, catching a flash of movement as Jill lead Nemesis on a wild goose chase in the distance, before refocusing much closer, a spark of an idea forming. “Keep clearing what you can,” he barked to Dwight. “I’ll be right back.” He sprinted for the edge of the Eyrie, boots skidding on broken rubble as he bolted out into the courtyard. His eyes locked onto the small ring of rusted iron fencing around one of the grave plots — nonsensical little monuments the Entity had scattered like décor. They looked sturdy; hopefully it would be enough. He crashed into the closest post, gripped the bars, and wrenched . They didn’t give easily. But he didn’t stop. Anger fueled him. At David. At himself. At the Entity. At the design of this entire place. With a shout and a final kick, a chunk of the wrought iron fencing snapped free with a pained squeal. Felix turned and ran — twisted metal gripped like a weapon — back into the dark. Dwight had stopped trying to clear the top of the pile. Too unstable. Every time he shifted something, it felt like the rest of it wanted to come with. Instead, he’d gone back into his small tunnel, and set himself to widening it. Probably not the smartest idea he had all day, he mused, but they needed to get some kind of space around him and the top kept shifting around too damned much. Maybe from down here, Dwight could get some of the pressure off him so he could breathe easier. He had noted Felix’s unspoken concern almost immediately, and had double checked for himself. David was technically still breathing, if you could call it that. Small, insufficient wisps at far too high of a speed didn’t really instill confidence. But at least David was still trying. Dwight dug his way around the shallower end of the pile, working down past David’s left arm — thankfully not pinned under him — and opening a gap around his side. Thanks to the slab above, he had a nearly clear line down both sides of David’s torso, but couldn’t get much of the weight off without making the upper layers shift threateningly. He followed along the fabric of David’s jacket hem, sweeping away more debris and trying to get at the stones around the large piece pinning his torso in place. Every one that he managed to shift sent small streams of grit raining down around him, making him question every move. He didn’t really feel much like being buried alongside David. Outside the rubble, he could hear Felix storming back in, already calling on him to get out of the way. “Shift! Give me space — I don’t want to accidently hit you!” “Hit me? What are you —” “Get out ! Just MOVE .” Dwight barely managed to push himself backwards along his cramped tunnel before a chunk of metal speared through the space between a few stones. He yelped and yanked his arm out of the way, scampering out of the gap to see Felix trying to pry the stones up with what looked like a busted piece of fencing. He angled the fence piece, one end digging into the rubble while the other rested across a larger chunk. There wasn’t a lot of room to maneuver, and he had to reposition twice to keep from spearing David in the process before finally managing to settle it along the stones just above the slab. Trying to get under it would guarantee that he would stab David by accident. This way, at least he could get some of the weight off the compression layer. Possibly even enough to pull him loose entirely. “Alright.” He nodded. “When I say go, I need you to put everything on it. Don’t pull — press. Get as much weight behind it as you can.” Dwight looked dubious. “You realize I have the upper body strength of wet spaghetti, right?” “You don’t need it. Just put your weight into it. It doesn’t need to move much. I’d do it but I’ve seen you favoring that arm. You’re not going to be able to pull him free.” Dwight winced a bit, flexing against the throb in his arm, but nodded and moved to brace himself against the bar. Felix took his place at the gap he had carved out, easily slipping between the stones before calling out for him to start shoving. He leaned his whole weight into the bar — back bowed, knees shaking, blood dripping from his elbow — and couldn’t help but grin a bit as he felt something on the other side give way. Just a few inches. But it was something. Felix dove further into the pocket of space, immediately scraping aside whatever rubble remained over David’s chest and arm. Not all of it. There wasn’t room. But he could move . He could touch . He could see the stuttering rise and fall of David’s ribs. Hear the dry rasp of breath in his throat. It didn’t sound healthy, or even stable for that matter, but it was more than it had been. It would have to be enough. Between the two of them, they managed it. The slab lifted just enough — Dwight grunting, legs shaking, throwing everything he had into the bar — and Felix got an arm under David’s shoulders and pulled . The pressure gave with a low, grinding groan. As soon as the weight shifted, the rest of the stones seemed to settle on their own, collapsing inward to fill the space he left behind. A few sharp edges scraped his legs on the way out. Ripped cloth. Skin. Nothing critical. Nothing a simple medkit couldn’t fix. He had gotten lucky in that aspect, the rubble along his legs having been no worse off for him than a hook injury. Probably less so. Even then, it didn’t matter. They had him. Felix dragged David clear, huffing from the exertion as he laid him out on the flat stone behind them. Dwight dropped the bar and scrambled over, falling to his knees beside them. “David—? Come on, man — talk to me—” He reached out and shook his shoulder — gently, but desperate — and the stillness was deafening. “Is he —? “ “Pulse is still there. He’s just not breathing right.” Felix set to easing David’s shoulders up to rest along his lap. He tipped his head back carefully, opening his airway the way he’d seen medics do, the extra space granting a light wheeze from him as his eyelids fluttered lightly. “There you go,” Felix muttered, brushing dust from his face. “You’re not allowed to check out on me now.” Dwight let out a strained huff as he hovered nearby, clearly not sure how to be of help. He looked down at David’s arm, bits of skin visible through the torn sleeve of his jacket. The damage was clear. Bruises were already forming in lurid shades of red and violet, crawling up from the wrist to the shoulder in uneven splotches. It didn’t look broken, but that arm was going to scream when it finally woke back up. Maybe it was better that he was still out. “I don’t understand why this keeps happening. It was never like this...” “I thought you guys were always fighting to not die in these trials?” “Not like this!” Dwight stared at David, trying to will him to wake up. “There was structure. Ritual. Patterns. You’re too new to the Fog; you wouldn’t know. But this kind of shit? This never happened. I don’t know what to DO anymore.” “Think maybe punching him will help too?” Dwight flinched, a light flush blooming across his face. “I said I was sorry —” Felix flashed him a quick smirk, betraying the attempt at defusing the tension, and Dwight visibly uncoiled a bit. “This is all so screwed up now. I didn’t know what else to do...” “No, you made the right call.” Felix ran a hand over David’s chest, frowning at the uneven, shallow movements, the edges of a thought pressing in on his mind. “Although... it might not be the worst idea...” “You want me to hit him? Are you out of your mind?” “No, I mean... hang on.” Felix shifted his grip and pressed two fingers into the muscle just above David’s injured shoulder, digging straight into the bruising that mottled whatever skin was visible. David jerked like he’d been shocked — a raw, hoarse inhale tearing out of him with the pain. His chest hitched violently against it, the air locked behind tightly clenched muscles for a moment, before finally breaking free with an ugly ragged sound. A second wet gasp tore out of him like his body didn’t want to breathe but couldn’t stop trying. Another followed, then a third — until the motion collapsed into a raw, hacking cough that curled him hard onto his side and out of Felix’s grip. His lungs were fighting the return. Like they’d forgotten what breathing felt like and were relearning by force. Each inhale was a frantic jerk, each exhale a failed sob. He choked on air like it was water, body spasming from the effort. Felix muttered something in a language Dwight couldn’t quite catch as he knelt beside David, one hand braced lightly against his back, rubbing slow circles in an attempt to ease the shaking. It wasn’t much, but it helped steady the worst of the spasms. David was curled in on himself, breaths still ragged, but the panic was bleeding off. Slowly. Painfully. Like steam venting from a pressure valve. Dwight sank back on his heels, finally letting the tension leave his shoulders. His hands were trembling — still streaked with dust and blood — and he balled them tightly against his lap trying to steady himself. Felix reached for his neck, fingers searching for his pulse — and David flinched hard, jerking back with a hitched breath as his eyes flew open. Alarm flickered there for a split second, chased quickly by confusion... then heat. Embarrassed fury, sharp and defensive. He shoved Felix’s hand away with a clumsy swat, the effort barely coordinated. “‘m fine,” he wheezed — the words cracked, shredded, broken in half by another coughing fit. His body twitched as he dragged in a breath, followed by another, each one a battle. Still, he braced a hand beneath himself, stubborn to a fault, trying to push upright even as his whole frame trembled from the strain. Felix didn’t even wait for him to finish coughing before the fury hit. “You idiot,” he snapped, voice tight and sharp with leftover panic. “ How long were you having trouble breathing in there? Why didn’t you say anything?! I would have changed the entire approach! You damn near got yourself killed! What the hell were you thinking?!” David, still catching up to the reality of being not dead , didn’t flinch. His legs shook under him, right arm cradled close, but his jaw locked stubbornly as he shoved himself up another inch. “We don’t have time for this,” he growled, eyes lit with a glare so sharp it looked like he planned to punch the Fog itself into submission. He staggered to his feet like a man with something to prove, wobbly legs carrying him limping towards the nearest doorway. Dwight scrambled to steady him, reaching an arm out — but David batted him away, stubbornly dragging one foot past the other in a crooked shuffle toward the edge of the Eyrie. “ Unbelievable, ” Dwight muttered, half to himself. Watching the man push forward on half a lung, a jacked-up arm, and the raw fuel of unprocessed rage, he couldn’t help the breathless laugh that broke loose. “Stubbornness and pure spite. That’s all he’s running on.” The universe seemed to agree. As if on cue, David’s eyes rolled back mid-step, knees buckling, his body finally cashing the debt his bravado had racked up. Dwight caught him just in time, locking his good arm around David’s shoulders. “Whoa — gotcha, gotcha—!” Felix moved in without a word, and together they got him back onto the sand, David groaning and muttering curses as they lowered him. He tried to fight it, but even the fight had gone soft now—just slurred protest and shallow breath. He was done. Felix leaned in close, his voice low, taut with fury still burning under the relief. “ Stay down , idiot. Don’t you ever do that to me again. Do you hear me?” His hands were firm against David’s shoulders, grounding and unrelenting. “You think you’re invincible, but I damn near just watched you die . I am not doing that again.” David blinked up at him, bleary and barely present. The words hit somewhere behind his eyes, too close and too loud, but he didn’t have the strength to push them away. The last thing he heard before the black overtook him was Felix’s voice — sharp, scolding, and laced with something bitter underneath that bloomed a fuzzy sense of guilt somewhere in the back of his mind. Ch 5 – Fallout The fire crackled low, casting warped shadows against the crumbling stone around camp. Soft amber light edged the survivors in flickers of warmth—on cloth, on skin, on all the things they weren’t saying. Dwight sat with his back to one of the ruined archways, his arm cradled in a makeshift sling — someone’s spare flannel, frayed at the edges. Not pain, exactly. What ache had survived the trip through the Fog had since settled into a dull stiffness that made every motion feel like a negotiation. Jill crouched by the fire, half-watching the embers, half-glaring at the others like she couldn’t decide whether to scold them or just throw a stick and call it even. "I leave for one trial," she muttered, breaking the silence. "And you clowns manage to trigger a cave-in? What the hell even happened in there?" Dwight opened his mouth. Closed it again. Thought better of the whole idea. The tension was high enough, and he didn’t feel like having it turn against him. The fire held its breath. Crackled, but barely. Its glow pushed shadows into the corners of the old stone ring, gilding faces that weren’t looking at each other, only at the flicker between them. Across the flames, Felix sat on the bare stone — not quite hunched, but folded tight. Hands limp in his lap. Legs pulled in close. Coiled, like movement would be too much. Like stillness was the only way to stop everything from slipping sideways. The firelight glinted off his face in brief, uneven flashes — too bright, too sharp. His gaze stayed fixed on the flames, but there was nothing soft about it. Quiet fury, bottled perfectly behind his eyes. David sat opposite him. Slouched, smaller than usual, shoulders drawn in like a man trying to disappear into the earth one vertebra at a time. His jacket was off, tossed somewhere behind him. Shirt sleeves shoved up to the elbows, exposing the bruises that tracked his arm in raw, splotchy streaks — violet and wine-dark, angry even in the Fog’s forgiving light. He’d barely said two words since his second impromptu nap. Claudette had checked his ribs with gentle fingers. Meg had given him a mug of something warm and vaguely sweet. Someone — he couldn’t even remember who — had wrapped a blanket around his shoulders like a cape he didn’t ask for. Now and then, his eyes flicked toward Felix — never long, never steady. A glance. A ghost of a look. Then back down. Like if he met those eyes for real, something might fracture beyond repair. The silence wasn’t just awkward. It was dense. Suspended. Like the Fog itself was watching, waiting to see who would break first. No one spoke. Even Jill — who could usually be counted on to cut tension with a well-placed snort or tactical sarcasm — had gone still. Her earlier irritation had banked into silence, burning low like the coals. But her eyes kept straying to Felix. Not worried. Not exactly. Just... tracking. He only looked calm to someone that wasn’t familiar with quite rage, and she was waiting to see if the fault line in him would hold. The longer the silence went on for, the heavier it felt. It settled between them — dense, restless. Lacking in the peace that should have come with healing wounds and building fatigue. Thick enough that it felt like a fifth presence in the circle, sitting between them with smoke on its breath. Unable to stand the tension, David shifted. He set the mug down beside him with a soft ceramic clink, fingers lingering around it like maybe, if he was lucky, it would swallow him whole. He stared at the fire. Then the cup. Then the dirt. Finally, cautiously, like he had to test the air first — he cleared his throat. “...You gonna yell at me again?” Felix didn’t look over. Didn’t blink. “No,” he said softly, firelight catching on the leftover dust that still coated his hair. “I got it out of my system.” A pause. “...You sure?” “No.” David tried to take a deeper breath to steady himself — he regretted it immediately. His ribs flared under the bruises, a deep ache that echoed through his torso. He winced lightly against the sensation, shifting his pose the smallest amount to take the excess pressure off. The next trial was going to suck if he couldn’t even take a deep breath without folding in half. That was, assuming Felix didn’t just cripple him before the night was done. Not that he wouldn’t have deserved it. Felix glanced over, the motion subtle but sharp. His expression was unreadable, carved into something just shy of composed. A careful arrangement of clear restraint — like someone trying very hard not to say something they’d regret. “I’m not mad you got hurt,” His voice didn’t rise. Didn’t waver. “I’m mad you hid it. From me. ” That landed. Not just as a reprimand — there was a strong tone of betrayal under it. David’s gaze dropped instantly, back to the fire, like maybe if he stared hard enough the flames would explain what the hell he was supposed to say. “...Didn’t think it mattered,” he muttered, after too long. Felix’s jaw flexed — just once. Quiet. Controlled. Just enough to say: wrong answer. “I didn’t want you two to panic,” David said, softer now. His voice scraped low, like it was trying not to shake. “Didn’t think it’d help if I made it a thing. Figured... if I kept quiet, we’d all get through it faster. You guys didn’t need the extra stress in the moment.” He hesitated, then added — too quiet: “Didn’t think anyone would notice if I just didn’t say anything.” He had meant it as a shield. A half-hearted excuse, a clumsy patch on the crawlspace he’d built to hide the worst of it. It landed more like a door slamming shut. Felix turned his head — slow, sharp, deliberate. “Do you think I wouldn’t have eventually noticed?” he asked, the firelight caught in his eyes, gleaming through the crack in his voice. “You seriously think I wouldn’t care?” David flinched internally. Not from pain — that, at least, had dulled to a manageable throb under the Fog’s numb haze. But that ? That low, even voice from Felix — no raised tone, no sarcasm, just open truth dropped on him like a stone. That hurt something deep in his chest that flared worse than the damage to his ribs had. “It’s not that,” David said quickly, too quickly. The words spilled like he was trying to plug the hole with excuses. Felix didn’t interrupt. Didn’t argue. Didn’t save him from the silence that followed. Somehow, that was worse. David raked a hand back through his hair, fingers catching in dried blood along the way and twitching lightly against the pull, like the sting was deserved. “I’ve always handled my shit,” he muttered. “That’s what I do. ” His voice hardened, not in anger, but defense. Old habits surfacing like bruises under skin. “People don’t need to babysit me. They need me solid. If I fall apart — what the fuck happens to the rest of you?” It was a deflection. A wall built out of duty. It sounded flimsy even as he had said it. “And what happens if you die?” Quiet. Even. “You think that won’t break something?” David didn’t answer. He couldn’t. Because suddenly, he wasn’t sure. The silence stretched again — not empty this time, but taut. Like a wire pulled too tight between two bodies while everyone else was pretending they couldn’t hear it hum. Jill nudged a stick in the fire with the toe of her boot. She watched the sparks jump like it was the most fascinating thing she’d seen all day. Anything to keep her eyes off them . Dwight, on the other side of the circle, was rewrapping the same strip of cloth around his arm for the third time. Not because it needed fixing. Because it gave his hands something to do. Because stillness felt dangerous. Neither of them spoke. Neither dared to. Not while the fallout was still settling. Not while whatever thread tethered Felix and David to each other was straining like that — so close to snapping it felt like the fire should’ve gone out from the pressure alone. Felix’s voice broke the silence, flat and quiet. “You would have been brought back.” David looked up at that — mouth parting, maybe to protest, maybe to argue. Felix didn’t let him, raising a hand to cut off his reply. “But not all of you.” The words were precise . Surgical in their restraint. Carefully chosen. David stared at him. Felix’s eyes didn’t meet his this time. They drifted toward the fire — like whatever he was about to say was easier to aim at the flames. “You know what happens,” he said. “They come back, sure. But they don’t always remember. They forget names. Details. Whole people .” His voice didn’t shake. But something in it cracked — as if it had to be said before it turned to ash in his throat. “I’ve watched it happen,” Felix said, his voice softer now. Thinner. “I’ve watched someone stare straight through their own teammate like they were a stranger. Because the Fog took that thread from them. And it never came back.” David swallowed. Hard. His throat felt tight, raw — The words somehow lodging there instead of landing clean. Felix looked at him then. Really looked. Not through the fire. Not past him. At him. His eyes were sharp, but there was something exposed there too — something he wasn’t used to letting show. “If you’d died today,” he said quietly, “And I had to sit across from you tomorrow while you acted like we’d never even met—” He stopped. Didn’t finish. Didn’t need to. The thought hung there, complete on its own. David felt the burn settle low in his gut. This had never been about the injury at all. This had been about loss for Felix. Not the kind that the survivors were used to — bleeding, screaming, that moment of panic before getting brought back — but the kind that erases . There was a sudden pressure behind David’s ribs — something inside that had cracked open and didn’t know how to close again. Too wide. Too raw. A guilt that filled every available space. His hands moved without aim — one pressing instinctively to his injured arm, the other twisting in his lap like it was trying to find something to hold on to. He fixed his gaze on the fire again, too uncomfortable to keep facing Felix. The man’s anger at him had hurt before, sure, but now it hurt in a way that mattered . He didn’t know what to do with that. His voice came out small and bare. Fragile in a way none of them were used to hearing from him. “I figured... worst case, I’d reset. Take the hit. Come back fresh.” He swallowed, the firelight highlighting the shame that flushed up the sides of his neck. “I didn’t think anyone would—” He stopped himself. Breathed. Tried again. “I didn’t mean to scare you.” It wasn’t eloquent. Wasn’t grand. But at least it was honest, even if it hurt just to say it. David finally glanced up — a flick of the eyes, barely enough to register, but full of a silent, desperate wish that something in Felix’s expression would have softened by now. That this could be over. That the worst had already passed. He wasn't that lucky. Felix’s face hadn’t changed. There was no rage. No heat. Just the weight of disappointment. And that was somehow worse. “You didn’t just scare me,” His voice calm, matter of fact, “You almost erased yourself. ” David, who had thrown himself in front of killers, taken hits without flinching, bled out beneath hooks and crawlspaces and basement stairs — who thought he knew what damage felt like — had no armor for that. He gaze wilted back down into the fire. And for the first time since they’d pulled him out of the rubble, he felt like maybe he hadn’t actually made it out at all. The silence that followed could’ve been carved with a knife. Even the fire seemed to crackle more quietly now—its usual hisses and pops reduced to something hesitant, like it was trying not to intrude. David looked ready to dissolve into the stone beneath him. Felix was still watching, still unreadable — eyes narrowed, posture tight, like he hadn’t decided if this counted as closure or just damage control. CRACK The fire split open with a sudden snap as a log shifted. The sound rang longer than it should have, snapping through the quiet like a warning shot. Dwight jumped so hard he nearly dropped the marshmallow stick he hadn’t actually used in the last twenty minutes. It clattered against the stone, and he fumbled to pick it up like it mattered. Jill, who had been studiously examining a patch of gravel like it held the secrets to the universe, finally cleared her throat. “Well,” she said lightly, a forced cheer pushing through the awkward tension, “remind me never to leave you boys unsupervised again.” Felix blinked and startled slightly, like he’d forgotten anyone else was there. David exhaled, shoulders slumping. Tension bleeding out like someone had finally released the pressure valve around his lungs. “You miss all the fun, Jill,” Dwight muttered, forcing a grin. “You chose to run Nemesis around for half the trial.” “Well, someone needed to.” Jill tossed a pebble at his boot. “If I’d known you were gonna start a landslide while I was out playing fetch with Frankenstein, I’d have brought snacks.” Felix let out a quiet huff. Possibly a laugh. Possibly a sound of exhausted despair. Hard to say. David just scrubbed both hands over his face, like he wanted to erase the last ten minutes from existence by sheer force of will.
